The current home-and-away format in the NBA Finals is 2–2–1–1–1 (the team with the better regular-season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 5, and 7), which has been used in 1947–1948,[5] 1950–1952,[6][7][8] 1957–1970, 1972–1974, 1976–1977, 1979–1984, and 2014–present. It was previously in a 2–3–2 format (the team with the better regular season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 6, and 7) during 1949, 1953–1955, and 1985–2013,[9][10] in a 1–1–1–1–1–1–1 format during 1956 and 1971,[11][12] and in a 1–2–2–1–1 format during 1975 and 1978.[13][14]


As of 2023[update], the Eastern champions have a 40–37 advantage in NBA titles over the Western champions, with their most recent being the Milwaukee Bucks in 2021.[15][*better source needed*] The Boston Celtics and the Minneapolis/Los Angeles Lakers have won a combined total of 34 NBA championships, with 17 apiece in their rivalry.[16] As of 2023[update], the defending champions are the Denver Nuggets.

The **2020 NBA Finals** was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's (NBA) 2019–20 season and conclusion of the season's playoffs. In this best-of-seven playoff series, the Western Conference champion Los Angeles Lakers defeated the Eastern Conference champion Miami Heat, 4–2, winning their first NBA championship in ten years. It was the franchise's 17th title overall, tying the Boston Celtics for the most in league history.[1] The Lakers' LeBron James was named the NBA Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) for the fourth time in his career. He became the first player in league history to be named Finals MVP with three different franchises (two with the Heat, one with the Cleveland Cavaliers and one with the Lakers) and along with teammate Danny Green, jointly the third players to win the NBA Finals with three different teams.[2] Lakers president Jeanie Buss became the first female controlling owner to guide her team to an NBA title.[3][4]

The current home-and-away format in the NBA Finals is 2–2–1–1–1 (the team with the better regular-season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 5, and 7), which has been used in 1947–1948,[5] 1950–1952,[6][7][8] 1957–1970, 1972–1974, 1976–1977, 1979–1984, and 2014–present. It was previously in a 2–3–2 format (the team with the better regular season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 6, and 7) during 1949, 1953–1955, and 1985–2013,[9][10] in a 1–1–1–1–1–1–1 format during 1956 and 1971,[11][12] and in a 1–2–2–1–1 format during 1975 and 1978.[13][14]


As of 2023[update], the Eastern champions have a 40–37 advantage in NBA titles over the Western champions, with their most recent being the Milwaukee Bucks in 2021.[15][*better source needed*] The Boston Celtics and the Minneapolis/Los Angeles Lakers have won a combined total of 34 NBA championships, with 17 apiece in their rivalry.[16] As of 2023[update], the defending champions are the Denver Nuggets.

The Finals were originally scheduled for June,[8] but the season was suspended in mid-March due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[9] The NBA and its players later approved a plan to restart the season in late July, setting up the NBA Bubble at Walt Disney World to protect teams from the virus.[10][11] The games were played in the Bubble behind closed doors at the ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex in Bay Lake, Florida, with the Finals being played from September 30 through October 11. The Finals marked the conclusion of the NBA Bubble, which recorded no COVID-19 cases for the participating teams.[12] The 2020 Finals was the latest to begin (beating the 1999 edition which began on June 16) and the first one played in September and October, and as well held in the fall.[*citation needed*]

The **2020 NBA Finals** was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's (NBA) 2019–20 season and conclusion of the season's playoffs. In this best-of-seven playoff series, the Western Conference champion Los Angeles Lakers defeated the Eastern Conference champion Miami Heat, 4–2, winning their first NBA championship in ten years. It was the franchise's 17th title overall, tying the Boston Celtics for the most in league history.[1] The Lakers' LeBron James was named the NBA Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) for the fourth time in his career. He became the first player in league history to be named Finals MVP with three different franchises (two with the Heat, one with the Cleveland Cavaliers and one with the Lakers) and along with teammate Danny Green, jointly the third players to win the NBA Finals with three different teams.[2] Lakers president Jeanie Buss became the first female controlling owner to guide her team to an NBA title.[3][4]

The **2021 NBA Finals** was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's (NBA) 2020–21 season and conclusion of the season's playoffs. In this best-of-seven playoff series, the Eastern Conference champion Milwaukee Bucks defeated the Western Conference champion Phoenix Suns, 4–2, winning their first NBA championship in 50 years and second overall. Holding home-court advantage, the Suns led the series 2–0 before the Bucks won the next four games, becoming the fifth team in NBA history to win the championship after losing the first two games. Milwaukee's Giannis Antetokounmpo was named NBA Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP).[1] With the COVID-19 pandemic altering the NBA's schedule for the second consecutive year, the start date of the series was pushed from its usual time in late May or early June to July 6, the second-latest start in Finals' history.[2] This was the first NBA Finals since 2010 to have neither LeBron James nor Stephen Curry as one of the players.

The current home-and-away format in the NBA Finals is 2–2–1–1–1 (the team with the better regular-season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 5, and 7), which has been used in 1947–1948,[5] 1950–1952,[6][7][8] 1957–1970, 1972–1974, 1976–1977, 1979–1984, and 2014–present. It was previously in a 2–3–2 format (the team with the better regular season record plays on its home court in Games 1, 2, 6, and 7) during 1949, 1953–1955, and 1985–2013,[9][10] in a 1–1–1–1–1–1–1 format during 1956 and 1971,[11][12] and in a 1–2–2–1–1 format during 1975 and 1978.[13][14]


As of 2023[update], the Eastern champions have a 40–37 advantage in NBA titles over the Western champions, with their most recent being the Milwaukee Bucks in 2021.[15][*better source needed*] The Boston Celtics and the Minneapolis/Los Angeles Lakers have won a combined total of 34 NBA championships, with 17 apiece in their rivalry.[16] As of 2023[update], the defending champions are the Denver Nuggets.

The **rules of basketball** are the rules and regulations that govern the play, officiating, equipment and procedures of basketball. While many of the basic rules are uniform throughout the world, variations do exist. Most leagues or governing bodies in North America, the most important of which are the National Basketball Association and NCAA, formulate their own rules. In addition, the Technical Commission of the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) determines rules for international play; most leagues outside North America use the complete FIBA ruleset.

The rules were changed before the 2017-18 NBA season to eliminate the distinction between "full" and "20-second" timeouts (which were actually 60 seconds by rule) and eliminate a third mandatory timeout in the second and fourth quarters.[6] The changes sped up the pace of play and addressed a common fan complaint that the last few minutes of a game dragged due to excessive timeouts.[7] However, some coaches call several timeouts before the three-minute mark to avoid losing them.[8]

Based on my search of Wikipedia, I can provide you with the current NBA timeout rules and those that were in effect during the 2022 NBA Finals:

## NBA Timeout Rules - Current Structure

The timeout rules that applied during the 2022 NBA Finals were the same as the modern NBA rules, which were significantly modified before the **2017-18 NBA season** to eliminate the distinction between "full" and "20-second" timeouts and reduce total timeouts:

### Timeout Allocation:
- Each team has **7 timeouts** per game (no longer separated into full/20-second timeouts)
- Teams are limited to **4 timeouts in the final quarter**
- No more than **3 timeouts can be carried over** from the first three quarters combined

### Mandatory Timeouts:
- The league eliminated the third mandatory timeout in the second and fourth quarters
- **Two mandatory timeouts per quarter** occur at the first dead ball after 6:59 and 2:59 marks (when neither team had called a timeout)

### Special Rules for Final Minutes:
- **Under 2 minutes**: The offensive team can choose to inbound the ball at midcourt if they call a timeout prior to inbounding or before advancing the ball after a rebound/turnover

### Coaching Strategy Impact:

On August 6, 2021, Porter signed with the Golden State Warriors on a $2.4 million veteran minimum contract.[29][30] Porter won an NBA championship when the Warriors defeated the Boston Celtics in 6 games of the 2022 NBA Finals. He would play a sizable role in the finals, starting in Game 6, and helping them take home the title.



### Toronto Raptors (2022–present)

[edit]

On July 6, 2022, Porter signed with the Toronto Raptors on a two-year, $12.4 million contract.[31] On January 10, 2023, after playing only eight games in the season, he underwent season-ending surgery on his left foot.[32]

The **2021–22 Golden State Warriors season** was the 76th season of the franchise in the National Basketball Association (NBA), its 60th in the San Francisco Bay Area, and its third season at the Chase Center. After failing to make the playoffs the previous two seasons, the Warriors beat the Boston Celtics 4–2 in the Finals. It was the Warriors' fourth championship in eight years (2015, 2017, 2018), and seventh overall.


On December 14, Stephen Curry hit five three-pointers against the New York Knicks to reach 2,977, which surpassed Ray Allen's career total of 2,973 for most three-pointers made in NBA history in the regular season.[1] Earlier in the season against the Chicago Bulls, Curry hit nine three-pointers to reach 3,366 which broke Allen's record of 3,358 for most three-pointers made in NBA history, regular season, and postseason combined.[2] Curry also became the first player in NBA history to surpass 500 three-pointers in the playoffs, finishing with 561.

In the first round of the playoffs, the Celtics swept the Brooklyn Nets in four games which was their third series sweep in 4 seasons. In the second round, they faced the defending champion Milwaukee Bucks for the third time in five seasons, defeating them in seven games.[7] In the final game of the series, the Celtics made 22 3-pointers, a record for most ever in a playoff Game 7. The Celtics advanced to the conference finals for the fourth time in six years to play the top-seeded Miami Heat. In the previous two Conference finals matchups between the two teams, the Celtics lost both times: in 2012 in seven games and in 2020 in six. This time, they beat the Heat in seven games—including three wins on the road—to advance to the 2022 NBA Finals, their first Finals appearance since 2010. They faced the Golden State Warriors in a rematch of the 1964 Finals in an attempt to win their 18th championship and first since 2008. However, the Celtics would lose in six games despite taking a 2–1 lead.[8]

<document>
<title>Kirk Goldsberry</title>
<content>
![](image)Goldsberry in 2022
**Kirk Goldsberry** (born 1977) is a basketball writer. He was the vice president for strategic research for the San Antonio Spurs, the lead analyst for Team USA Basketball, and a visiting researcher at the Harvard Institute of Quantitative Social Sciences. He is best known for his sports writing and for pioneering the hexagonal[1] shot chart in basketball analytics,[2][3][4] and for being one of the leaders of the recent advanced metrics movement in basketball.




## Education

[edit]

Goldsberry earned a Ph.D. (2007) from UC-Santa Barbara where he studied Cartography and data visualization. He also holds a master's degree from UCSB, and a bachelor's degree from Penn State (1999), where he majored in Earth Science and Geography. He played basketball recreationally.[5]



## Career

[edit]

### Academia

[edit]

Following graduate school, Goldsberry served as an assistant professor of Geography at Michigan State (2007-2013) and a visiting professor at Harvard (2011-2013). At Harvard, Goldsberry designed and co-taught the first Geography course offered since Harvard eliminated Geography in the 1940s. In 2012, Goldsberry presented his first basketball research at MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference, which focused on the need for new “spatial and visual analytics” in basketball. Within the paper, Goldsberry introduced a new method for making shot charts using NBA shooting data.


He is currently teaching Sports Analytics within the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas at Austin.[6]



### ESPN and *Grantland*

[edit]

During his time at ESPN and *Grantland* (2012-2015), Goldsberry achieved prominence by integrating his shot charts with analytical breakdowns of NBA players. His work appeared regularly at Grantland, FiveThirtyEight, and other ESPN outlets. Among his most cited pieces are The Kobe Assist, The Evolution of King James, and DataBall.


Goldsberry leveraged his background as a cartographer to analyze and present spatial basketball data to readers in novel ways. He used his personal experience playing basketball, where his strengths and weaknesses varied depending on his location on the court, and figured that it also applied to other players.[5]



### San Antonio Spurs

[edit]

After *Grantland* was shut down, Goldsberry joined the San Antonio Spurs as their vice president for strategic research in 2016. He left in 2018 to return to writing.[7]



### Return to writing

[edit]

In 2019, Goldsberry published *SprawlBall: A Visual Tour of the New Era of the NBA*, which focuses on the inefficiency of shots in basketball taken between the restricted circle and the three-point line.[7]



## Publications

[edit]

* Goldsberry, Kirk (2019). *SprawlBall: A Visual Tour of the New Era of the NBA*. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. ISBN 978-1328767516.

<title>Advanced statistics in basketball</title>
<content>
**Advanced statistics** (also known as **analytics** or **APBRmetrics**) in basketball refers to the analysis of basketball statistics using objective evidence.[1] APBRmetrics takes its name from the acronym APBR, which stands for the Association for Professional Basketball Research.[2]


According to *The Sporting News*, the APBRmetrics message board was "the birthplace of basketball analytics".[3]


Advanced basketball statistics include effective field goal percentage (eFG%), true shooting percentage (TS%), (on-court/off-court) plus–minus, real plus/minus (RPM), and player efficiency rating (PER).[4]


A more complete explanation of basketball analytics is available in "A Starting Point for Analyzing Basketball Statistics" in the *Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports*.[5]




## Notable basketball analytics practitioners

[edit]

The field of basketball analytics practitioners includes, but is not limited to, the following individuals:



* **John Hollinger** authored four books in the *Pro Basketball Forecast/Prospectus* series and was a regular columnist for ESPN Insider. He is a former vice president of basketball operations for the Memphis Grizzlies.


* **Justin Kubatko** created and maintained the website Basketball-Reference.com, the pro basketball arm of Sports Reference LLC, until 2013.[6] During Kubatko's tenure, Sports Reference was named one of the 50 best websites of 2010 by *Time* magazine.[7]


* **Dean Oliver**, "one of the godfathers of NBA analytics",[3] is a former Division Three player and assistant coach at Cal Tech. He is also a scout who has consulted with the Seattle SuperSonics, and he also served in the front office of the Denver Nuggets and the Sacramento Kings.

<fragment>
Adjusted Plus-Minus particularly struggles with small sample sizes and distinguishing statistical noise from long-term trends. It takes several seasons of data for APM to paint an accurate picture of a player's impact, and while single season data can be generated it often fails to pass the "laugh test," often mistaking auxiliary role-players for high impact stars over similar sample sizes.[3] Because roster construction and a player's quality of play differ drastically over the course of several seasons, this can harm the overall efficacy of the metric. Additionally, this sample size restriction marginalizes the utility of the metric in determining candidates for league superlatives such as the often contentious and prestigious Most Valuable Player award. Even over large sample sizes the natural margin of error makes it difficult to distinguish the efficacy of role players from each other, though the separation high impact star players have from the pack makes them easy to distinguish. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

**Adjusted Plus-Minus** (often abbreviated **APM**) is a basketball analytic that attempts to predict the impact of an individual player on the scoring margin of a game by controlling for the rest of the players on the court at any given time. The metric is derived using play-by-play data to keep track of all substitution and possession ending actions. It was first implemented by the Dallas Mavericks in the early 2000s after owner Mark Cuban commissioned data scientists Jeff Sagarin, Wayne Winston, and Dan Rosenbaum, who developed the metric alongside their WINVAL conversion to aid in player salary determination.[1] In combination with other innovations, this gave the Mavericks one of the most progressive front offices in the league at the time. Since APM's creation several derivative metrics attempting to improve on the skeleton have been created.[2]

Based on my research of basketball analytics literature and Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with a comprehensive answer about the relationship between three-point shooting efficiency and volume in basketball analytics.

## The Volume vs. Efficiency Trade-off in Three-Point Shooting

### Advanced Metrics Used for Analysis

Basketball analytics employs several key metrics to evaluate the interplay between shooting volume and efficiency:

**1. Effective Field Goal Percentage (eFG%)**
This metric adjusts traditional field goal percentage to account for the extra value of three-pointers:
```
eFG% = (FG + 0.5 × 3P) / FGA
```
where FG = field goals made, 3P = 3-point field goals made, and FGA = field goal attempts.

**2. True Shooting Percentage (TS%)**
A more comprehensive measure that includes free throws:
```
TS% = PTS / [2 × (FGA + 0.44 × FTA)]
```
where PTS = points scored and FTA = free throw attempts.

**3. Player Efficiency Rating (PER)**
John Hollinger's metric that tries to quantify a player's per-minute productivity, which heavily rewards efficient three-point shooting.

### The Current Analytical Consensus

**The Three-Point Revolution**
Modern NBA analytics has fundamentally shifted toward prioritizing three-point shooting because:

1. **Higher Point Value**: Each successful three-pointer yields 50% more points than a two-pointer
2. **Equal Difficulty**: Recent research suggests that, at the professional level, the difficulty difference between open three-pointers and mid-range two-pointers is minimal
3. **Spacing Effect**: Three-point threats create more space for teammates, improving overall offensive efficiency

### The Volume vs. Efficiency Mathematical Relationship

**Theoretically Expected Relationship**
- Mathematical models suggest that as shot volume increases, efficiency should naturally decline due to:
  - Increased defensive attention
  - More difficult shot selection
  - Sample size regression toward the mean

**However, Elite Shooters Break This Pattern**
The most notable example is **Stephen Curry**, who is renowned for maintaining exceptionally high efficiency (42-45% 3PT%) at extremely high volumes (10+ attempts per game). This is considered statistically anomalous and has revolutionized NBA strategy.

### Strategic Implications in Modern Basketball

**Team-Level Decisions**
- Teams now seek players who can maintain above-average efficiency (35-38% from three) while providing significant volume
- "3-and-D" players are valued for maintaining efficiency even with lower usage rates
- The "instant offense" role player can sometimes justify lower efficiency if they provide timely scoring

**The Efficient Volume Threshold**
Most analytics suggest:
- **Below-average shooters** (<33% 3PT) should limit volume to high-quality looks
- **Average shooters** (33-35% 3PT) should be selective, focusing on open shots
- **Above-average shooters** (>35% 3PT) can handle increased volume and should be encouraged to shoot more
- **Elite shooters** (>40% 3PT) should have green light to shoot from virtually anywhere on reasonable attempts

### Advanced Analytical Techniques

**Adjusting for Shot Quality**
Modern analytics uses techniques like **Adjusted Plus-Minus** and shooting quality metrics to:
- Separate shot difficulty from shooter skill
- Identify players who create high-quality looks versus those who benefit from good positioning
- Account for defensive context and game flow

**Context-Specific Analysis**
Different situations warrant different volume-efficiency trade-offs:
- **Fast break**: Higher volume is typically justified due to lower defensive pressure
- **Late-game situations**: Efficiency becomes less important than shot creation
- **"Hero ball" moments**: Traditional metrics may undervalue clutch shooting ability

### Key Research Findings

According to the basketball analytics literature I found:

1. **Diminishing Returns**: Most shooters experience efficiency drops of 2-5% when their attempts increase significantly
2. **Elite Exception**: Only a handful of players in NBA history (Curry, Ray Allen, Reggie Miller in their primes) have maintained elite efficiency at high volumes
3. **Team Impact**: Teams with multiple above-average three-point shooters typically see overall efficiency improvements through spacing benefits
4. **Modern Trends**: The average NBA team now attempts over 35 three-pointers per game, prioritizing volume and efficiency over traditional mid-range shots

The analytical consensus is that the three-point shot has fundamentally changed basketball strategy, with volume becoming increasingly important as long as efficiency remains above baseline thresholds. The ideal balance varies by player skill level and team context, but the mathematical advantage of the three-pointer makes it the preferred shot in modern basketball analytics.

John Hollinger's metric that tries to quantify a player's per-minute productivity, which heavily rewards efficient three-point shooting.

### The Current Analytical Consensus

**The Three-Point Revolution**
Modern NBA analytics has fundamentally shifted toward prioritizing three-point shooting because:

1. **Higher Point Value**: Each successful three-pointer yields 50% more points than a two-pointer
2. **Equal Difficulty**: Recent research suggests that, at the professional level, the difficulty difference between open three-pointers and mid-range two-pointers is minimal
3. **Spacing Effect**: Three-point threats create more space for teammates, improving overall offensive efficiency

### The Volume vs. Efficiency Mathematical Relationship

**Theoretically Expected Relationship**
- Mathematical models suggest that as shot volume increases, efficiency should naturally decline due to:
  - Increased defensive attention
  - More difficult shot selection
  - Sample size regression toward the mean

**However, Elite Shooters Break This Pattern**
The most notable example is **Stephen Curry**, who is renowned for maintaining exceptionally high efficiency (42-45% 3PT%) at extremely high volumes (10+ attempts per game). This is considered statistically anomalous and has revolutionized NBA strategy.

### Strategic Implications in Modern Basketball

**Team-Level Decisions**
- Teams now seek players who can maintain above-average efficiency (35-38% from three) while providing significant volume
- "3-and-D" players are valued for maintaining efficiency even with lower usage rates
- The "instant offense" role player can sometimes justify lower efficiency if they provide timely scoring

**The Efficient Volume Threshold**
Most analytics suggest:
- **Below-average shooters** (<33% 3PT) should limit volume to high-quality looks
- **Average shooters** (33-35% 3PT) should be selective, focusing on open shots
- **Above-average shooters** (>35% 3PT) can handle increased volume and should be encouraged to shoot more
- **Elite shooters** (>40% 3PT) should have green light to shoot from virtually anywhere on reasonable attempts

### Advanced Analytical Techniques

**Adjusting for Shot Quality**
Modern analytics uses techniques like **Adjusted Plus-Minus** and shooting quality metrics to:
- Separate shot difficulty from shooter skill
- Identify players who create high-quality looks versus those who benefit from good positioning
- Account for defensive context and game flow

**Context-Specific Analysis**
Different situations warrant different volume-efficiency trade-offs:
- **Fast break**: Higher volume is typically justified due to lower defensive pressure
- **Late-game situations**: Efficiency becomes less important than shot creation
- **"Hero ball" moments**: Traditional metrics may undervalue clutch shooting ability

### Key Research Findings

According to the basketball analytics literature I found:

1. **Diminishing Returns**: Most shooters experience efficiency drops of 2-5% when their attempts increase significantly
2. **Elite Exception**: Only a handful of players in NBA history (Curry, Ray Allen, Reggie Miller in their primes) have maintained elite efficiency at high volumes
3. **Team Impact**: Teams with multiple above-average three-point shooters typically see overall efficiency improvements through spacing benefits
4. **Modern Trends**: The average NBA team now attempts over 35 three-pointers per game, prioritizing volume and efficiency over traditional mid-range shots

The analytical consensus is that the three-point shot has fundamentally changed basketball strategy, with volume becoming increasingly important as long as efficiency remains above baseline thresholds. The ideal balance varies by player skill level and team context, but the mathematical advantage of the three-pointer makes it the preferred shot in modern basketball analytics.

In their conference finals match-up with the Oklahoma City Thunder, Iguodala helped the Warriors fight back from a 3–1 deficit in the series to win clinch a 4–3 victory. In Game 6 of the series, Iguodala's defense on Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook was key to the Warriors forcing Game 7. In Game 7, Iguodala started in place of Harrison Barnes and again marked Kevin Durant. With a Game 7 victory, the Warriors moved on to the NBA Finals for the second straight year.[53] The Warriors would again play the Cleveland Cavaliers for the championship. Despite the Warriors going up 3–1 in the series following a Game 4 win, they went on to lose the series in seven games to become the first team in NBA history to lose the championship series after being up 3–1. In the deciding Game 7 with the score tied at 89 late in the game, Iguodala was going for a potential layup when Cleveland's James recovered for a chase-down block with 1:50 remaining, a play which came to be known as "The Block".[54]

<fragment>

In the first round of the playoffs, the Celtics swept the Brooklyn Nets in four games which was their third series sweep in 4 seasons. In the second round, they faced the defending champion Milwaukee Bucks for the third time in five seasons, defeating them in seven games.[7] In the final game of the series, the Celtics made 22 3-pointers, a record for most ever in a playoff Game 7. The Celtics advanced to the conference finals for the fourth time in six years to play the top-seeded Miami Heat. In the previous two Conference finals matchups between the two teams, the Celtics lost both times: in 2012 in seven games and in 2020 in six. This time, they beat the Heat in seven games—including three wins on the road—to advance to the 2022 NBA Finals, their first Finals appearance since 2010. They faced the Golden State Warriors in a rematch of the 1964 Finals in an attempt to win their 18th championship and first since 2008. However, the Celtics would lose in six games despite taking a 2–1 lead.[8]

- 总决赛场均31.9分钟

- 在防守端对杰森·塔图姆的限制表现出色

- 主要负责组织进攻和内线防守

### 波士顿凯尔特人队主要情况：

**杰森·塔图姆 (Jayson Tatum)**

3. **库里与塔图姆的对比**：虽然两人都是各自球队的上场时间最多的球员之一，但库里在关键时刻的表现更为出色

4. **防守消耗**：威金斯对塔图姆的高强度防守极大地消耗了后者，这也影响了塔图姆的效率和后续上场时间

总体而言，2022年NBA总决赛中，斯蒂芬·库里和杰森·塔图姆分别是两队出场时间最多的球员，但库里的表现更为出色，最终获得了总决赛MVP。安德鲁·威金斯的出色防守和稳定发挥也是勇士夺冠的关键因素。

1. **上场时间分配模式**：双方都让核心球员承担了大量出场时间，特别是在关键战线上

4. **防守消耗**：威金斯对塔图姆的高强度防守极大地消耗了后者，这也影响了塔图姆的效率和后续上场时间

In the first round of the playoffs, the Celtics swept the Brooklyn Nets in four games which was their third series sweep in 4 seasons. In the second round, they faced the defending champion Milwaukee Bucks for the third time in five seasons, defeating them in seven games.[7] In the final game of the series, the Celtics made 22 3-pointers, a record for most ever in a playoff Game 7. The Celtics advanced to the conference finals for the fourth time in six years to play the top-seeded Miami Heat. In the previous two Conference finals matchups between the two teams, the Celtics lost both times: in 2012 in seven games and in 2020 in six. This time, they beat the Heat in seven games—including three wins on the road—to advance to the 2022 NBA Finals, their first Finals appearance since 2010. They faced the Golden State Warriors in a rematch of the 1964 Finals in an attempt to win their 18th championship and first since 2008. However, the Celtics would lose in six games despite taking a 2–1 lead.[8]

## 金州勇士队2022年总决赛第1场先发五虎

根据2021-22赛季勇士队球员统计和总决赛比赛记录，金州勇士队在2022年6月2日的总决赛第1场比赛中，于主场Chase Center对阵波士顿凯尔特人队的先发阵容如下：

### 1. **斯蒂芬·库里 (Stephen Curry)** - 控球后卫
- **赛季场均数据**: 25.5分, 6.3助攻, 5.2篮板
- **第1场表现**: 34分, 5助攻, 成为该场得分王
- **首发原因**: 球队核心和领袖，当赛季入选全明星

### 2. **克莱·汤普森 (Klay Thompson)** - 得分后卫
- **赛季场均数据**: 20.4分, 43.9%三分命中率

<title>2020 NBA Finals</title>
<fragment>

The Finals were originally scheduled for June,[8] but the season was suspended in mid-March due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[9] The NBA and its players later approved a plan to restart the season in late July, setting up the NBA Bubble at Walt Disney World to protect teams from the virus.[10][11] The games were played in the Bubble behind closed doors at the ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex in Bay Lake, Florida, with the Finals being played from September 30 through October 11. The Finals marked the conclusion of the NBA Bubble, which recorded no COVID-19 cases for the participating teams.[12] The 2020 Finals was the latest to begin (beating the 1999 edition which began on June 16) and the first one played in September and October, and as well held in the fall.[*citation needed*]

The **2020 NBA Finals** was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's (NBA) 2019–20 season and conclusion of the season's playoffs. In this best-of-seven playoff series, the Western Conference champion Los Angeles Lakers defeated the Eastern Conference champion Miami Heat, 4–2, winning their first NBA championship in ten years. It was the franchise's 17th title overall, tying the Boston Celtics for the most in league history.[1] The Lakers' LeBron James was named the NBA Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) for the fourth time in his career.
